m:
Kütahya Province (Turkish: Kütahya ili) is a province in the Aegean region of Turkey. Its area is 11,634 km2, and its population is 580,701 (2022). In 1990, Kütahya had a population of 578,000.
The neighboring provinces are Bursa to the northwest, Bilecik to the northeast, Eskişehir to the east, Afyon to the southeast, Usak to the south, Manisa to the southwest and Balıkesir to the west.
The capital city of the province is Kütahya.

Q411571: Aizanoi, Latinized as Aezani, was an Ancient Greek city in western Anatolia. It was located at the site of the modern village of Çavdarhisar, near Kütahya, on both sides of the Penkalas river, c. 1,000 m (3,300 ft) above sea level. The city was an important political and economic centre in Roman times; surviving remains from the period include a well-preserved Temple of Zeus, a combined theatre-stadium complex, and a round building, probably a macellum, inscribed with a copy of the Price Edict of Diocletian. The city fell into decline in Late Antiquity. In 2012 the site was submitted for inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Q20470665: Kütahya Great Mosque, also known as Yıldırım Beyazıt Mosque, is the only imperial mosque in Kütahya. It was begun when Prince Bayezid (Yıldırım) was governor of Kütahya (1381–1389) and completed by his son Prince Musa Çelebi after Bayezid was captured at the Battle of Ankara.
Q6022256: Kütahya Castle is a castle from the Byzantine period in the city of Kütahya.
Q942877:
The Penkalas Bridge is a Roman bridge over the Penkalas (today Kocaçay), a small tributary of the Rhyndakos (Adırnas Çayı), in Aezani, Asia Minor (Çavdarhisar in present-day Turkey).
The 2nd-century AD structure was once one of four ancient bridges in Aezani and is assumed to have been the most important crossing-point due to its central location in the vicinity of the Zeus temple and the direct access it provided to the Roman road to Cotyaeum (Kütahya). According to reports by European travellers, the ancient parapet remained in use as late as 1829, having been replaced today by an iron railing.
Around 290 m upstream, another well-preserved, almost identical five-arched Roman bridge leads across the Penkalas.
Q20471303:
Kütahya Archaeological Museum is a museum in Kütahya, Turkey.
The museum is located in the Vacidiye Medrese, a historical medrese (Islamic school) building commissioned by the Germinyanid ruler Umur in 1314. It is next to Kütahya Ulu Mosque ("Grand mosque") at 39°25′02″N 29°58′34″E. In 1965 it was opened as a museum. After a period of restoration it was reopened on 5 March 1999.
The building material is cut stone and the portal is of Seljukid style. There are nine rooms. The exhibits span the Paleolithic, Chalcolithic, Bronze Age, Hittite, Phrygian, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Seljukid and Ottoman eras. The oldest items are painted ceramics from Hacılar.
One interesting item is a sarcophagus of a supposed Amazon, a rare specimen.
Q20476251:
Rüstem Pasha Medrese (Turkish: Rüstem Paşae Medresesi) 
is a medrese building, located in Kütahya, Turkey. It was rebuilt after the original building, which was built by Ottoman statesman and grand vizier Rüstem Pasha in 1550. It was partly demolished in the 1930s.
Q20470671: Çinili Mosque in Kütahya was built by the painter Ahmet Yakupoğlu and opened for worship in 1975. Covered inside and out with Kütahya tiles, it has become one of the city's symbols.
Q6032910: İshak Fakih Mosque in Kütahya, dated 1433, is a late Germiyanid work built by İshak Fakih, a noted local scholar of Islamic law. It has cut-stone and brick walls and a showy façade; its three-part porch has cut stones framed with red brick, and one section of it serves as a tomb.
Q6036038: Timurtaş Pasha Mosque (also called Takkeciler or Takvacılar Mosque) is a mosque near the Small Bedesten in Kütahya.
Q6100614: Seyitömer Mound lies 24–25 km north-west of Kütahya as the crow flies, north-west of Seyitömer village, within the reserve land of the Seyitömer lignite mine. It measures 150 x 140 metres and is 24 metres high, with a flat area of about 2,000 m² on top.
Q31189944: Bülbül Mescidi is a small mosque in the Mecidiye quarter of central Kütahya, thought to date from the early 19th century. Its builder and date are uncertain, but court records list it as the Yakup Çavuş Mescidi, so it existed before 1830 and is said to have been built by Yakup Çavuş.
Q98091629: Tavşanlı Great Mosque is in the Tavşanlı district of Kütahya. The first mosque, of unknown date, is thought to have been built by Arslan Bey in the Germiyanid period; the present mosque was built on its foundations in the 19th century under Abdulhamid II.
Q61074659: The Martyr Standard-Bearer Mehmetçik Monument stands near Zafertepeçalköy in the Altıntaş district of Kütahya and is dedicated to those who fell in the Turkish War of Independence.
Q125404771: Eğdemir Bath, also called Eydemir or Elvan Bey Bath, is a hamam in Kütahya.
Q131738634: Lala Hüseyin Pasha Bath is a hamam in Kütahya.
Q131739131: Kemer Bath is a hamam in Kütahya.
Q21526496: Kütahya Clock Tower stands in central Kütahya.
Q6071250: The Dumlupınar War of Independence Martyrs' Memorial in the Dumlupınar district of Kütahya was built by the Ministry of Culture in memory of the Turkish soldiers who fell at the Battle of Dumlupınar. It opened on 30 August 1992, the 70th anniversary of the Great Offensive.
Q6056682: The Kossuth House Museum (also called the Hungarian House) is an 18th-century Turkish house in Kütahya, open to visitors since 1982; it belonged to Şeyh Bedreddin Efendi. It displays belongings of the lawyer Lajos Kossuth, a leader of the Hungarian Revolution who lived here in 1850–1851, and objects of Hungarian culture. Kossuth wrote his draft constitution for Hungary in this house.
